sections.heading: Putting your kingdom before my own name
sections.text: Sovereign God, I want my heart to be taken up with your cause, not my own. I come to you freely because this is your work: bring your kingdom into every place where evil still holds people captive. Make your name honored, and let that be enough for my joy. Teach me to care more about your glory than about being noticed, successful, or secure.
theological_themes: God’s sovereign rule over his kingdom
Seeking God’s glory above personal ambition
Freedom to ask God for what aligns with his will

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches his disciples to pray first for the Father’s name to be honored and for his kingdom to come. This grounds the prayer’s movement away from self-interest and toward God’s reign.
Paul frames all of life around doing everything for God’s glory. That supports the desire that personal joy be tied to God being honored rather than to personal gain.

sections.heading: Longing for others to know you
sections.text: I worship you because you are God. I want other people to know you too—not just to hear true things about you, but to recognize your worth, love you, praise you, and find their joy in you. For the sake of your name, bring sinners home to yourself.
theological_themes: Worship as delight in who God is
Evangelistic longing for sinners to come to God
God’s name as the reason for mission

scripture_references.connection: This psalm asks for God’s blessing so that his way and salvation may be known among all nations. It connects worship, joy, and the spread of God’s saving rule among peoples.
Paul shows that people call on the Lord through hearing the gospel, and that preaching is part of God’s means of bringing salvation. This fits the prayer’s longing that sinners be brought to God.

sections.heading: Trusting you where I cannot see how people will change
sections.text: When I look at the conversion of others with only human reason, it can feel impossible. I cannot open blind eyes, soften hard hearts, or make anyone love Christ. But you can do what I cannot. This is your cause, and it honors you when people are saved. So I ask you to do great things that only you can do.
theological_themes: Human inability to produce spiritual conversion
Salvation as God’s work and God’s glory

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes unbelief as spiritual blindness and says that God gives the light of the knowledge of his glory in Christ. This directly supports the prayer’s confidence that only God can bring saving sight.
Jesus teaches that no one comes to him unless the Father draws him. This grounds the prayer’s dependence on God rather than on human persuasion alone.

sections.heading: Offering myself for your work
sections.text: Lord, use me however you want. Do with me what you know is best. I am not asking you to build my platform or protect my comfort; I am asking you to advance your kingdom in this world. Let your good purposes move forward, and bring many people to Jesus.
theological_themes: Ministry as participation in God’s mission
Christ as the one to whom people must be brought

scripture_references.connection: The risen Jesus sends his people to make disciples on the basis of his authority. This supports the prayer’s desire to be used in the advance of Christ’s mission.

Paul counts his life as secondary to finishing the ministry he received from the Lord Jesus. This illuminates the prayer’s willingness to be used by God without making self-preservation the highest aim.

sections.heading: Spending my life for people to come to Jesus
sections.text: Please let me see a day when many are gathered to Christ. Give me a large-hearted concern for people’s souls, not a small or casual one. Make me willing to suffer, and even to die, if that would serve your saving purposes. And while I am alive, help me work for you with all the strength you give me. In health or weakness, keep me from wasting my time. Make my life useful for your cause, not centered on my own. Father, please answer this prayer.
theological_themes: Faithful labor in both strength and weakness
A life spent for God’s kingdom rather than self

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes laboring with God’s energy to present people mature in Christ. This supports the prayer’s request to work to the limit of God-given strength for the spiritual good of others.
Paul speaks of sharing not only the gospel but his own life with those he served. This fits the prayer’s willingness to spend oneself, not merely perform religious tasks.
Paul wants Christ to be honored in his body whether by life or by death. This gives biblical shape to the prayer’s willingness to live or die for the advancement of Christ’s cause.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original phrase about places 'where Satan reigns' could be misunderstood as dualistic, as if Satan’s power were equal to God’s. I rendered it as real spiritual captivity under evil while preserving God’s sovereignty and the biblical theme of deliverance from darkness.

The original’s desire to be 'willing to die' for the conversion of many could sound like reckless self-destruction if isolated. I framed it as costly surrender to God’s saving purposes, in line with biblical patterns of sacrificial ministry.
The phrase 'all men' was rendered as 'other people' and 'many people' to preserve the original universal evangelistic concern in contemporary English.
significant_interpretive_choices: I treated 'thy cause' mainly as the advance of God’s kingdom through the salvation of sinners and the honor of God’s name, because the prayer repeatedly connects God’s cause with people being brought to Jesus.
I interpreted 'the eye of reason' as unaided human judgment that cannot explain or produce conversion, rather than as a rejection of reason itself.
I kept the prayer’s strong emphasis on God’s sovereign action in conversion while also preserving the original’s request that God would use the praying person in active ministry.
